body.text: The New Brunswick research and development tax credit gives claimants performing eligible SR&ED a 15% fully refundable credit under section 59 of New Brunswick's Income Tax Act, claimed on Schedule 360 and administered by the CRA. It stacks with federal SR&ED investment tax credits but, as government assistance, reduces the federal SR&ED expenditure pools.

Canada operates one of the world's most comprehensive, rules-based fiscal regimes for supporting industrial research and innovation, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Administered jointly through statutory provisions of the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945, by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) with policy oversight from the Department of Finance Canada, the program delivers two distinct fiscal mechanisms: an immediate, indefinitely carryforwardable deduction against business income under Section 37 of the ITA, and a volume-based Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA that provides up to a 35% refundable tax credit for eligible corporations and a 15% basic tax credit for all other claimants. When stacked with provincial and territorial research and development (R&D) tax credits—and harmonized with direct federal innovation grants such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP)—the Canadian regime substantially lowers the after-tax net cost of performing technical experimentation in Canada.

Between late 2024 and March 2026, Canada enacted the largest structural expansion of the SR&ED program in decades. Initiated in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, expanded in Budget 2025 (Canada Strong, tabled November 4, 2025), and enacted into law upon receiving Royal Assent on March 26, 2026 via Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), these statutory reforms apply retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024). Specifically, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (generating up to $2,100,000 in annual refundable cash), broadened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out, restored the full SR&ED eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 (which had been repealed since January 1, 2014), and introduced an elective Pre-Claim Approval mechanism alongside artificial intelligence administrative streamlining. Concurrently, at the provincial level, Quebec's Budget 2025–2026 (tabled March 25, 2025) abolished eight legacy innovation tax measures and consolidated its system into the size-neutral, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025.
1. Executive Summary and Ledger of Key Statutory Parameters

A rigorous audit of Canadian R&D tax law requires separating historical rules (specifically the 2014–2024 restriction era) from the statutory regime currently in force under the Income Tax Act following the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026. Furthermore, practitioners must strictly distinguish between the calculation of the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) and the calculation of qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible to earn an ITC under subsection 127(9). An expenditure may be deductible against business income under Section 37 without necessarily producing an ITC in the same amount under Section 127.

body.text: 2. Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Scientific Eligibility Criteria
2.1 The Statutory Text of Subsection 248(1)

All federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada rest upon the legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the federal Income Tax Act (first added to subsection 248(1) in 1996, having previously resided in Regulation 2900). Notably, while Bill C-15 overhauled the financial parameters and expenditure categories of the SR&ED program in 2026, Parliament left the core definition in subsection 248(1) unchanged.

Under subsection 248(1), "scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls into one of three foundational branches:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view.
Paragraph 248(1)(b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. In practice, industrial SR&ED claims in Canada are predominantly filed under the experimental development branch, which explicitly encompasses incremental technological improvements alongside major breakthroughs, provided the work seeks to advance technological knowledge rather than merely applying existing engineering knowledge.

body.text: 2.2 Eligible Support Work under Paragraph 248(1)(d) vs. Excluded Work under Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)

Because industrial research rarely occurs in isolation from engineering implementation, paragraph 248(1)(d) extends the definition of SR&ED to include work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive statutory categories: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research. For any of these eight activities to qualify under paragraph 248(1)(d), two strict statutory conditions must be satisfied simultaneously: the work must be (1) commensurate with the needs and (2) directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs 248(1)(a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work performed for its own sake—or in excess of what is required to construct, execute, or validate an experimental hypothesis—is disallowed. Furthermore, contract or shop-floor work performed by manual trades (such as electricians, welders, or mechanics) that does not fall within the eight enumerated categories in paragraph 248(1)(d) cannot be claimed directly as support work, though it may qualify as SR&ED overhead and other expenditures under the Traditional Method if it is directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the ITA establish an express statutory exclusion against seven categories of commercial, routine, or non-scientific activity. Work falling into these seven paragraphs cannot be claimed as SR&ED: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes (alterations to aesthetic form, finish, or proportions); and (k) routine data collection. As the CRA emphasizes in its Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives, the distinguishing factor between eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) and excluded work under paragraphs 248(1)(e)–(k) is purpose (why the work was conducted). For example, data collection or testing conducted as part of normal operations or quality assurance is excluded under paragraphs (f) and (k) even if the resulting data later proves useful to an R&D team, whereas data collection or testing carried out specifically to directly support an active experimental development investigation is eligible under paragraph 248(1)(d).
2.3 Evolution of Administrative Guidance: The Five Questions vs. The "Why" and "How" Requirements

Historically, following the Department of Finance's May 1985 Budget Papers (which introduced "experimental development" to exclude routine engineering), the issuance of Information Circular IC 86-4 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development) in 1986 (revised through IC 86-4R3 in 1994), and Chief Justice Bowman's landmark Tax Court of Canada judgment in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, the CRA evaluated technical eligibility through five sequential questions published in its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (first published in 2012 and revised in 2015).

On August 13, 2021, the CRA archived the 2015 policy and promulgated the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives, consolidating the five common-law questions into two overarching operational requirements: the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement. As confirmed by the CRA and subsequently by the Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, this administrative update did not alter the legal standard under subsection 248(1); rather, it mapped the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria directly onto the statutory language.

headers: Core Legal & Technical Standard Required of the Claimant

cells: Question 1: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?

An insufficiency or limitation in available scientific or technological knowledge (comprising both the internal resources of the business and publicly accessible standard practice) such that a competent professional cannot determine in advance whether or how the objective can be achieved.
Question 4: Did the process result in a technological advancement?

The work must seek to generate conceptual knowledge (theories, prediction models, or technological know-how explaining how constituents interact) rather than mere factual measurements. Commercial or technical failure still satisfies this test if hypotheses are eliminated and knowledge is gained.
Question 2: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?
Formulating a testable statement, proposed method, or architectural concept consistent with known scientific facts designed to overcome the identified uncertainty.
Question 3: Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?
The "How" Requirement (Steps 2 & 3: Testing by Experiment/Analysis and Logical Conclusions)

Executing a systematic investigation via controlled experiment or analysis, observing and measuring empirical results, drawing logical conclusions, and iteratively modifying the hypothesis. Unguided "trial and error" or applying workarounds using known methods is disqualified.
Question 5: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed?
Maintaining contemporaneous evidence (e.g., design of experiments, lab notebooks, trial run logs, software commit logs, failed test data, and analysis) generated as the work progresses.

body.text: Nuances of Technological Uncertainty in Software, AI, and Engineering

A critical audit pitfall identified in the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work is conflating business or project uncertainty or a lack of internal familiarity ("we had not done it before") with scientific or technological uncertainty ("the field does not know whether this works"). Acquiring existing knowledge or know-how through employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring external consultants, or purchasing proprietary technology does not meet the "Why" requirement. Similarly, if a technical obstacle is ignored or circumvented using a workaround based on available knowledge, or if economic cost targets alone are cited without imposing an underlying technological limitation, the work is ineligible. Instead, the CRA identifies seven specific characteristics indicating that available technological knowledge is insufficient in experimental development: (1) existing design methods are not applicable; (2) requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards; (3) there are too many variables or unknowns; (4) parameters or conditions are outside the normal operating range; (5) the nature of the problem is evolving; (6) data is not readily available; or (7) there are interlocking constraints.
3. Federal SR&ED Financial Architecture: Deductions, ITC Rates, and Phase-Out Mechanics

Calculating a federal SR&ED claim requires executing two sequential, mathematically distinct computations: first, determining the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under Section 37 (Form T661, Part 3); and second, determining the SR&ED Qualified Expenditure Pool and resulting Investment Tax Credits under Sections 127 and 127.1 (Form T661, Part 4, and Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)).
3.1 Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada in a taxation year may accumulate eligible SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada in a running pool. Unlike ordinary capital cost allowance (CCA) classes that depreciate over multiple years, the entire year-end positive balance of the subsection 37(1) pool may be deducted immediately against business income in the current taxation year, or any discretionary portion (down to $0) may be deducted and the remainder carried forward indefinitely to offset business income in any future taxation year. When a deduction from the Section 37 pool creates or increases a corporate non-capital loss for the year, that non-capital loss can generally be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years under Section 111 of the ITA.

body.text: Taxability of ITCs and Negative Pool Balances (Paragraphs 12(1)(v) and 12(1)(t))

Because federal SR&ED ITCs claimed or refunded in Year 1 reduce the subsection 37(1) pool in Year 2 (and provincial R&D credits reduce the pool in Year 1), if a claimant deducts its entire Section 37 pool in Year 1 and has zero or minimal SR&ED expenditures in Year 2, the Year 2 pool balance will become negative. Under paragraph 12(1)(v) (operating in conjunction with paragraph 12(1)(t)), any negative balance in the subsection 37(1) pool at the end of a taxation year must be brought directly into net income for tax purposes in that year, and is then added back under paragraph 37(1)(c.1) so that the opening pool for the following taxation year is never negative.
Exceptions to Indefinite Carryforward and Foreign SR&ED Rules

Two statutory exceptions restrict the carryforward of the Section 37 pool. First, a partnership cannot carry forward a subsection 37(1) pool balance; the entire pool at the end of the partnership's fiscal period must be fully deducted in calculating partnership net income for that year. Second, under subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h) (amended by Bill C-15 via clause 37(6.1)(a)(i)(B) to encompass restored paragraph 37(1)(b) capital expenditures), where a corporation or trust undergoes a loss restriction event (such as an acquisition of control), its unused pre-acquisition SR&ED pool is reduced to nil unless specific business continuity and similar-business income conditions are satisfied. Additionally, current expenditures incurred on SR&ED carried on outside Canada cannot enter the subsection 37(1) pool (other than permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada as outlined in section 10.0 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy) and earn 0% ITCs, but remain deductible against business income in the year incurred under subsection 37(2).
3.2 Section 127 and 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates and Refundability Matrix

Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127(10.1), and Section 127.1 of the ITA, taxpayers earn an ITC calculated as a percentage of their Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for the taxation year. Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026 (effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024), the federal ITC rate and refundability structure across entity types is governed by the following statutory rules:

body.text: Statutory Nuance: Qualifying Corporations vs. Non-Qualifying CCPCs (Subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01))

A critical technical distinction in Section 127.1 governs the refundability of the 15% basic ITC for CCPCs whose qualified expenditures exceed their expenditure limit. Under subsection 127.1(2), a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" only if its taxable income for the preceding taxation year (together with associated corporations) does not exceed its "qualifying income limit". Under the post-December 15, 2024 rules amended by Bill C-15, the qualifying income limit ranges from $500,000 down to nil and phases out over the exact same $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital range (increased from $10,000,000 to $50,000,000).

If a CCPC is a qualifying corporation (other than an excluded corporation), not only is its 35% enhanced ITC 100% refundable on current expenditures and the PPA (and 40% refundable on capital expenditures under amended subparagraph (f)(i) of the definition of "refundable investment tax credit" in subsection 127.1(2)), but any 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is also 40% refundable. Conversely, if a CCPC is not a qualifying corporation (and not an excluded corporation), subsection 127.1(2.01) preserves 100% refundability on its 35% enhanced ITC for current expenditures and the PPA (and 40% refundability for capital expenditures), but any 15% basic ITC earned above its expenditure limit is 0% refundable (non-refundable). Any ITC refunded in a taxation year is deemed under subsection 127.1(3) to have been deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable, thereby reducing the unused ITC balance available to be carried back 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward 20 subsequent taxation years.
3.3 The $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Formulas

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, subsection 127(10.2) (for CCPCs) and subsection 127(10.6) (for ECPCs and electing CCPCs) establish a baseline annual expenditure limit of $6,000,000 (doubled from $3,000,000 for tax years beginning before December 16, 2024). Across an associated group of corporations (determined under section 256 of the ITA, including deemed association where one of the main reasons for separate existence is to multiply the expenditure limit or refundable ITCs), this single $6,000,000 expenditure limit must be shared and allocated annually using Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsections 127(10.21) and 127(10.3) (or subsections 127(10.61) to 127(10.64) for consolidated ECPC groups).
1. Prior-Year Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Default for CCPCs — Subsection 127(10.2))

Bill C-15 expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range for CCPCs from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000 (a $60,000,000 phase-out span). For a CCPC (and its associated corporations) with a full taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024, the annual Expenditure Limit (ELCCPC) is determined by the statutory formula:

In this formula, A is nil ($0) if the aggregate taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year is less than or equal to $15,000,000; or, in any other case, the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that prior-year aggregate taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000. Consequently, for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above $15,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced by $1 (a 10% reduction rate), reaching $0 once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000.
2. Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out Formula (Mandatory for ECPCs & Elective for CCPCs — Subsections 127(10.6) and 127(10.32))

To extend the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—defined in subsection 127(9) as public corporations resident in Canada that are not controlled by non-resident persons (even if all shares owned by non-residents were owned by a single person)—Parliament introduced a phase-out formula based on average annual gross revenue under subsection 127(10.6) (with existing subsection 127(10.6) renumbered as subsection 127(10.5)). Furthermore, under subsection 127(10.32), a CCPC may elect by filing the prescribed form to use this 3-year average gross revenue method instead of the taxable capital method.

Under subsection 127(10.6), the Expenditure Limit (ELRev) phases out linearly as the 3-year average annual gross revenue (Ravg) of the corporation (and its consolidated or associated group members for the preceding 3 fiscal years, regardless of whether they were associated throughout that entire period, with reasonable adjustments for intra-group sales of goods or services so that annual revenue reflects a single economic entity) increases from $15,000,000 to $75,000,000:

In this formula, B is the excess of Ravg over $15,000,000 (up to a maximum of $60,000,000), where Ravg is the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements for the 3 preceding fiscal years.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methods, and Specific Cost Rules
4.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (Subsection 37(8) and Regulation 2900)

When filing Form T661 for a taxation year, a claimant must elect on lines 160 or 162 to compute its SR&ED expenditures using either the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) or the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)). Pursuant to subsection 37(10) of the ITA, this election must be made when Form T661 is first filed for the taxation year and is irrevocable for that taxation year (though a claimant may choose either method in a subsequent taxation year).

body.text: Under the Traditional Method (ITR subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3)), overhead and other expenditures claimed on Line 360 must satisfy two mandatory tests: the Directly Related Test (requiring a direct linkage without an intervening step or intermediary to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED) and the Incremental Test (meaning the expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred). Allowable Traditional Method overhead items include utilities, supplies, travel and lodging in Canada for hands-on SR&ED employees, Canadian training costs for hands-on SR&ED staff (whereas training or travel for clerical/administrative support staff is disallowed as indirect), employer-paid related benefits and retiring allowances if directly related and incremental, and dedicated cloud computing clusters provisioned for experiments.
4.2 Deep Dive: The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), Salary Base, and Specified Employee Restrictions

Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations and subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) to (VI) of the ITA, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is equal to 55% of the claimant's salary base for the taxation year. While the Proxy Method eliminates the need to track and allocate individual overhead expenses, the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy and SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy enforce four strict statutory rules on the salary base:

First, under the Directly Engaged Requirement, only the portion of salary or wages of employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (hands-on experimentation, testing, commensurate support work, and direct technical supervision) can enter the salary base. Under the "All or Substantially All" (ASA) rule (ITR subsection 2900(5)), if a directly engaged employee spends 90% or more of their total working time in the taxation year on eligible SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages for the year qualifies. Amounts for extended vacation or sick leave, employer shares of related payroll benefits, retiring allowances, and stock option benefits under section 7 of the ITA are excluded from SR&ED salary or wages.

Second, under Mandatory Salary Base Exclusions (ITR subsection 2900(9)), while cash taxable benefits (or qualifying non-cash taxable benefits whose value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs, excludes GST/HST/PST unless no input tax credit is claimable, and whose underlying costs are not claimed as a business expense), enforceable or unenforceable bonuses, and remuneration based on profits paid to non-specified employees can be claimed as directly engaged SR&ED wages on Line 300, subsection 2900(9) strictly excludes four items from the Proxy Salary Base for all employees (both non-specified and specified): (1) taxable benefits under section 6 of the ITA; (2) bonuses; (3) remuneration based on profits; and (4) unpaid remuneration from a prior taxation year that was paid in the current taxation year (Line 310 of Form T661).

Third, Dual Statutory Caps apply to "Specified Employees" (Subsections 37(9)–(9.5) and ITR Subsections 2900(7)–(10)). A "specified employee" is an employee who is a specified shareholder (owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer. Specified employees are subject to two separate ceilings:

cells: Ceiling 1: Directly Engaged SR&ED Salary Cap (Form T661 Line 305 — Applies to both Traditional & Proxy Methods)

Bonuses and profit-based remuneration paid to specified employees are 100% disallowed (s. 37(9)). Eligible base salary is capped at 5 × YMPE (Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings under s. 18 of the Canada Pension Plan) for the calendar year in which the tax year ends, prorated by the number of days the individual was a specified employee in the year (s. 37(9.1)). Associated corporations (including deemed associated related individuals and partnerships under s. 37(9.5)) must share the 5 × YMPE cap by filing Form T1174 with certified directors' resolutions; otherwise, no amount may be claimed.
Ceiling 2: Proxy Salary Base Restriction (Form T661 Part 5 Lines 850–860 — Applies to Proxy Method PPA calculation)

The amount included in the Proxy Salary Base for each specified employee cannot exceed the lesser of: (1) directly engaged SR&ED salary (excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid amounts); (2) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, net of exclusions); or (3) 2.5 × YMPE prorated by the number of days employed in the tax year (2.5 × YMPE × [Days Employed / 365], with no proration for days the employee was not a specified employee). Associated corporations (and deemed associated related individuals/partnerships under ITR 2900(10)) must share the 2.5 × YMPE limit under ITR 2900(8).

body.text: Fourth, under subsection 2900(6) of the Regulations, an Overall Cap on the PPA ensures that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specific statutory deductions do not exceed total business expenditures deducted in the year:
Overall PPA Cap = A − B − C

In this formula, A is the total of all amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold, summed across all businesses if the claimant carries on more than one business); B is the sum of deductions claimed in the year under statutory sections 20 (e.g., CCA, interest, bad debts), 24 (ceasing business), 26 (banks), 30 (improving land for farming), 32 (insurance agents/brokers), 37 (SR&ED expenditures), 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and 104 (trusts) of the ITA; and C is the amount of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building. In general, the Overall Cap does not limit the calculated PPA so long as the claimant has deducted more than $55 of ordinary non-SR&ED business expenses (excluding the specified statutory deductions and building rent) for each $100 of eligible salary included in the salary base.
Compensation Traps: Dividends, Partnerships, and the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule (Subsection 78(4))

Founders or shareholder-researchers compensated via dividends rather than T4 employment salary have no salary or wages to claim; dividends are distributions of corporate surplus and generate $0 of SR&ED wages and $0 of PPA. Similarly, a member of a partnership cannot be an employee of the partnership for income tax purposes; any salary or wages paid to a partner is treated by the CRA as a distribution of partnership income and cannot be claimed as an SR&ED salary expenditure. Furthermore, under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, employee remuneration that is not paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred is deemed not to be an expenditure incurred in that year. It is excluded until the taxation year in which it is actually paid (identified on Line 310 of Form T661), where it is permanently excluded from the Proxy Salary Base under ITR 2900(9). Parallel rules require excluding other unpaid current SR&ED expenditures not paid within 180 days on Line 520 of Form T661 (and adding only 80% if applicable when paid in a subsequent year on Line 500).
4.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and ITC Recapture (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR (Traditional Method) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA (Proxy Method), a claimant may include 100% of the laid-down cost (original invoice cost plus customs and excise duties, transportation, storage, and other reasonable acquisition costs, or direct materials, labour, and production overhead for self-manufactured inventory) of physical and tangible raw materials, substances, or other items (solid, liquid, or gaseous) that compose the body of a tangible object at a given moment in the SR&ED process. Materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed (Line 320 — rendered virtually valueless) or transformed (Line 325 — incorporated into a prototype, custom product, or commercial asset) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, not when merely acquired or placed into inventory. While ambient utility heat, electricity, and boiler feed water are overhead expenses, energy used directly in endothermic reactions (chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, or metallurgical conversion) and process water that enters a chemical reaction to become part of an intermediate or final product qualify as materials consumed. Where SR&ED occurs simultaneously with commercial production (such as agricultural trials using animal feed, fertilizer, or pesticides), only the incremental cost attributable to the SR&ED study group qualifies.
The 20-Year ITC Recapture Regime (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA, recapture of SR&ED ITC is triggered when four conditions are met: (1) the claimant acquired a particular property (materials transformed or capital/shared-use equipment) in the current taxation year or any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years by subsection 127(36) for ITCs earned in 1998 and subsequent tax years); (2) the cost of the property was a qualified expenditure; (3) a percentage of that cost was included in computing the claimant's ITC; and (4) the claimant disposes of the property or converts it (or another property incorporating it) to commercial use in the taxation year.

When triggered, the recaptured amount is added directly to the claimant's federal Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion (and is added back to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the subsequent year). Under subsection 127(27), the recaptured ITC equals the lesser of: (a) the ITC earned on the cost of the particular property, and (b) the basic ITC percentage (15% for post-2013 expenditures; 20% for pre-2014 expenditures) applied to either the proceeds of disposition (for an arm's-length sale) or the fair market value (FMV) of the property at the time of conversion to commercial use or non-arm's length disposition.

Under subsection 127(32) ("meaning of cost"), a crucial audit distinction applies between in-house fabrication and subcontracted components: if a claimant manufactures an SR&ED prototype in-house, no recapture applies to the in-house salaries or overhead used to build the prototype (recapture is restricted to the cost of materials transformed). Conversely, if the claimant orders that custom component from an arm's-length supplier for $12,000 ($10,000 manufacturing/development cost plus $2,000 profit), the entire $12,000 purchase price is subject to recapture. Where intellectual property belongs to the payer from inception under an SR&ED contract, the payer is not "acquiring" property and no recapture applies if the IP is sold or commercialized. Finally, under the CRA's administrative de minimis rule, recapture is not applied where scrap proceeds or FMV upon conversion/disposition are less than 10% of the cost of the property.
4.4 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

For SR&ED performed on behalf of a claimant by an arm's-length contractor (Form T661 Line 370), 100% of the allowable contract expenditure enters the Section 37 pool, but only 80% enters the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool for ITC calculation. To qualify, the contracted work must be physically carried out in Canada, must cover basic research, applied research, experimental development, or commensurate support work (where the payer retains control and ownership/rights to the SR&ED performed), and must be paid or payable to a "taxable supplier" to prevent double-dipping. Under subsection 127(18), the contractor (performer) must reduce its own qualified SR&ED expenditures by any contract payment received or receivable from the payer. (Note: Consequential to the restoration of capital expenditures after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 repealed the former subsection 37(14) look-through rule and subsection 37(15) written notification rule for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024.)

Where SR&ED is performed by a person or partnership with whom the claimant does not deal at arm's length (NAL), the contract payment to the NAL performer is excluded from being a qualified expenditure of the payer. Unlike an arm's-length contractor hired solely for support work (who cannot claim SR&ED on standalone support work), an NAL performer contracted solely to perform support work is eligible to claim SR&ED expenditures and may either claim the ITCs itself or transfer its qualified expenditures (capped at its year-end qualified expenditure pool) to the NAL payer using Form T1146 under subsection 127(13). If materials or capital property are purchased from an NAL party, subsection 127(11.6) limits the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes to the actual cost incurred by the NAL seller, stripping out any intercompany profit.

Third-party payments (Form T1263) made to an approved corporation resident in Canada (Entity A), approved association (Entity B), approved university, college, or research institute (Entity C), or non-profit SR&ED corporation (Entity D) for SR&ED in Canada related to the claimant's business—where the performer controls the research and the claimant acquires a non-exclusive/preferential right to exploit the results—are claimed on a cash basis (in the year paid, including payments in kind valued at fair market value) and are 80% eligible for Section 127 ITCs.
4.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Enacted through Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the restoration of capital and lease expenditure eligibility applies to depreciable property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024, and lease payments that first become payable after December 15, 2024:

items: ASA Depreciable Capital Property (Paragraph 37(1)(b) and Subsection 127(9)): Depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, where at the time of acquisition the claimant intends to either (a) use the property during all or substantially all (≥90%) of its operating time in its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada, or (b) consume ≥90% of its value in SR&ED in Canada. While both new and used depreciable property meeting the ASA test can be included in the Section 37 deductible pool, only new depreciable property qualifies for the Section 127 ITC (as used or refurbished property is a prescribed excluded expenditure under ITR Section 2902). Land, inventory, goodwill, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are excluded under paragraph 37(8)(e), except for prescribed special-purpose buildings under ITR Section 2903. (Note: Outside the SR&ED capital regime, Bill C-15 also provides a 100% first-year CCA deduction for Class 50 computer hardware and systems software acquired after April 15, 2024, and available for use before 2027, as well as a 100% first-year deduction for eligible manufacturing and processing buildings acquired after November 3, 2025, where at least 90% of floor space is used for M&P activities.)

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9), ITR 2900(11), and ITR 2902(b)): New depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (excluding Prescribed Depreciable Property under ITR 2900(11) and General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture [GPOEF]) that does not meet the 90% ASA test but is used primarily (more than 50%) of its actual operating time for SR&ED in Canada qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE). Under First-Term SUE, if actual cumulative SR&ED operating hours exceed 50% of total operating hours from when the asset becomes available for use until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition, 25% (1/4) of the capital cost (calculated without section 21 borrowing costs) is deemed a qualified expenditure for Section 127 ITC purposes (claimed on Form T661 Line 504 and itemized in Part 6 Boxes 788–796 for the 20 most expensive SUE items). Under Second-Term SUE, if the asset qualified as First-Term SUE and cumulative actual SR&ED operating hours continue to exceed 50% from acquisition until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition, an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost qualifies for the Section 127 ITC (totaling 50% of capital cost across both periods). The capital cost of SUE does not enter the Section 37 pool and is instead depreciated via regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8.

Equipment Lease Costs (SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy): For lease costs first payable after December 15, 2024 (excluding building rent, unless a prescribed special-purpose building), eligibility depends on the elected method. Under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment (or GPOEF) is used ≥90% (ASA) of its operating time in SR&ED, 100% is claimed as a lease cost; if used <90%, the proportional SR&ED operating percentage is claimed on Line 360 as overhead if directly related and incremental. Under the Proxy Method (where GPOEF and land leases are excluded), if leased equipment is used ≥90% (ASA) in SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimable; if used >50% to <90% (primarily) in SR&ED, 50% of the lease cost is claimable; and if used ≤50%, 0% is claimable. For any taxation year straddling December 16, 2024, operating time percentages are measured strictly over total operating time after December 15, 2024.

body.text: 5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Nearly every Canadian province and the Yukon Territory offer supplementary R&D tax credits that build upon the federal SR&ED definition in subsection 248(1). Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal ITA, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (unless formally waived or renounced by the statutory deadline where permitted) constitute government assistance that reduces both the federal Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the federal Section 127 qualified expenditure pool. Importantly, under the Proxy Method, provincial R&D credits do not reduce the Proxy Salary Base used to calculate the federal 55% PPA; instead, the provincial credit is deducted from total qualified expenditures on Form T661 Part 4 (Lines 513–514) after the 55% PPA has been added. (Note: Under updated Form T661 Line 514 instructions, claimants exclude from Line 514 any provincial/territorial government assistance attributable to a capital expenditure for property acquired and available for use before December 16, 2024, that did not qualify federally.)

body.text: 5.2 Deep Dive: Jurisdictional Specifics and Recent Provincial Reforms
1. Ontario: Three-Tier Credit Architecture (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Ontario corporations with a permanent establishment in the province (and not exempt from tax under Part III of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario)) can stack three distinct credits administered by the CRA. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Schedule 566) provides an 8% refundable tax credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures and eligible repayments (yielding a maximum annual cash credit of $240,000 per associated group). (Note: Although a summary page on the CRA website lists sections 38–45 for both ORDTC and OITC, the statutory text of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) and the CRA's dedicated OITC technical guide confirm that the OITC is governed by Section 96, with expenditure limits in subsection 96(3.1), qualified expenditures in subsection 96(8), eligible repayments in subsection 96(12), and waivers in subsection 96(14)). Unlike the federal expenditure limit—which doubled to $6,000,000—Ontario's $3,000,000 OITC limit phases out when the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income exceeds $500,000 (becoming nil at $800,000), or when the prior-year specified capital amount (taxable paid-up capital) exceeds $25,000,000 (becoming nil at $50,000,000).

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38 to 45, Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit on all eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures with no expenditure ceiling. Because the OITC and OBRITC constitute government assistance for ORDTC purposes, the 8% OITC must be deducted from the Ontario expenditure base before multiplying by 3.5% (yielding an effective net ORDTC rate of 3.5% × (1 − 0.08) = 3.22% on the first $3,000,000). Unused ORDTC can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years, and recapture applies under section 45 (reported on Line 277 of Schedule 5) if property on which ORDTC was calculated is disposed of or converted to commercial use. Because unutilized ORDTC earned in a loss year is still considered by the CRA to "reasonably be expected to be received" and reduces the federal Section 37 and Section 127 pools immediately, subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) allows a corporation to deliver a written waiver of the ORDTC (in whole or in part) with its T2 return within 6 months of year-end (or on an amended return) to preserve its 35% cash-refundable federal SR&ED ITC.

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Schedules 568 and 569) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI), subject to a $20,000,000 annual qualified expenditure limit per associated group (maximum $4,000,000 refundable credit) and excluding payments funding wages of ERI employees connected to the paying corporation.
2. Quebec: The 2025–2026 Overhaul and Launch of the CRIC Regime

Quebec administers its corporate tax system independently through Revenu Québec. In the Quebec Budget 2025–2026 (presented March 25, 2025 by Finance Minister Eric Girard), the province enacted a major structural reform that applies to taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025. Specifically, Quebec abolished eight existing innovation tax measures: (1) the refundable Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7-V, which offered 30% for SMBs on up to $3,000,000 and 14% for large corporations above a $50,000 basic exclusion threshold); (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium; (3) the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research; (4) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9); (5) the industrial design component of the Tax Credit for Design (in-house and outside consultant); (6) the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services; (7) the Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers; and (8) the Tax Holiday for Foreign Experts.

Replacing these abolished credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, is the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC — Forms RD-222-V and RD-1029.8.CR). Unlike the legacy regime, CRIC is fully refundable for all eligible corporations regardless of size and modulates its rate strictly by expenditure volume: 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold, and 20% on all eligible expenditures beyond $1,000,000. The annual exclusion threshold is the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the basic personal amount under the Quebec personal income tax system applicable to each eligible employee, adjusted in proportion to the employee's time devoted to R&D and pre-commercialization activities. Crucially, CRIC expands the eligible expenditure base to cover (a) salaries and wages, (b) capital expenditures for acquiring depreciable property, and (c) 50% of subcontractor contracts (including universities, public research centres, research consortia, CCTTs, and CLTs), and extends technical eligibility beyond R&D to include pre-commercialization activities (regulatory validation tests, studies, and product design carried out in direct continuity with a Quebec R&D project).
3. Western and Atlantic Highlights: BC, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Atlantic Canada

In Western Canada, British Columbia (Form T666) provides a 10% credit under Part 6 (sections 97–103) of the BC Income Tax Act (refundable for CCPCs and, from tax years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, proposed/expanded to ECPCs up to the expenditure limit, and non-refundable above), and removed its September 1, 2027 sunset date so the credit is now permanent (with section 98 referring to an "eligible corporation"). Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant (AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970) provides an 8% fully refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base spending level (the average qualifying spending over the previous 2 years) and an enhanced 20% fully refundable payment on spending exceeding that 2-year base, up to a $4,000,000 annual spending cap. Saskatchewan (Schedule 403) provides a 10% credit (capped at $1,000,000 in combined credits per year) and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, doubled the CCPC refundable expenditure limit from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000. Manitoba (Schedule 380) provides a 15% credit (half refundable [7.5%] and half non-refundable [7.5%] for in-house R&D, and 15% fully refundable for R&D under contract with a qualifying institute; Manitoba did not follow the 2014–2024 federal disallowance of capital expenditures and allows 100% rather than 80% for contracts with Manitoba educational institutions). Finally, Nova Scotia (Schedule 340), New Brunswick (Schedule 360), Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule 301 / Form T1129), and Yukon (Schedule 442 / Form T1232) all provide 15% fully refundable R&D tax credits.
6. Interaction with Direct Grants (NRC IRAP) and End-to-End Stacking Methodology
6.1 Government Assistance and NRC IRAP Stacking Mechanics

Direct federal and provincial innovation grants—such as financial assistance from the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada's AgriInnovate Program, CanExport Innovation, NSERC, and regional development agencies such as FedDev Ontario and PrairiesCan, as well as forgivable loans whose repayment depends on future revenues or profits—constitute government assistance under subsection 127(9), paragraph 37(1)(d), and subsection 127(18) of the ITA. Government assistance and non-government assistance (amounts includable under paragraph 12(1)(x)) reduce both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar in the taxation year the assistance is received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received on or before the filing-due date. If assistance is later repaid, the repayment increases the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) and earns a non-refundable Section 127 ITC (at the ITC rate that applied when the assistance originally reduced the pool) that can be carried back 3 years or forward 20 years.

Crucially, when stacking NRC IRAP salary grants with the SR&ED Proxy Method, while the IRAP grant reduces the claimant's qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 515 of Form T661 Part 4, it does not reduce the directly engaged SR&ED Salary Base in Form T661 Part 5 on which the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated. Consequently, a company receiving an NRC IRAP grant on $400,000 of R&D wages still generates the full $220,000 PPA (55% of $400,000) before the IRAP grant is deducted from the combined expenditure pool.
6.2 Worked Numerical Calculation: Federal + Provincial + NRC IRAP Stacking (Ontario CCPC, Post-Dec 15, 2024 Tax Year)

Consider an Ontario-based Qualifying CCPC (prior-year taxable capital below $15,000,000; prior-year taxable income below $500,000) for a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024, governed by the Bill C-15 rules. The company elects the Proxy Method and incurs $580,000 of actual SR&ED outlays in Ontario: $400,000 in directly engaged non-specified employee salaries (Line 300), $100,000 in arm's-length Canadian subcontractor costs (Line 370), $30,000 in materials consumed (Line 320), and $50,000 for new ASA SR&ED capital testing equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 (100% SR&ED use), while receiving a $150,000 NRC IRAP salary grant (Line 515).

7. Landmark Judicial Precedents and Tax Court of Canada Jurisprudence

Because the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) turns on qualitative scientific and engineering principles, Canadian appellate and Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence governs technical eligibility disputes.

headers: Core Legal Holding and Audit Significance

cells: Established that a "systematic investigation or search" requires controlled, repeatable experiments, accurate measurements, and testing theories against empirical evidence where steps, changes, and results are carefully noted; unrecorded shop-floor trial and error without drawings, hypotheses, or test reports fails.
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520

Chief Justice Bowman formulated the foundational five-question test for SR&ED eligibility (technological risk/uncertainty, specific hypotheses, scientific method discipline, technological advancement in general understanding, and detailed contemporaneous record-keeping as work progresses).

Held that taxpayers must provide reliable evidence demonstrating that scientific research and repeatable testing occurred; while documentary evidence is strongly expected, contemporaneous written records are not an absolute legal condition if credible oral testimony and supporting evidence establish the work.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393 (aff'g 2000 D.T.C. 2372 (TCC))

Formally adopted the five Northwest Hydraulic questions at the appellate level. At trial (2000 DTC 2372), established that calling an external expert witness (Dr. Slonim) to retrospectively conjecture about software problems without calling the actual project manager who performed the work is fatal to proving SR&ED.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355
Reaffirmed the binding application of the Northwest Hydraulic / C.W. Agencies five-criteria framework and the taxpayer's evidentiary burden.
Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313 & Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6

Defined a "hypothesis" as "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial" (Joel Theatrical, para 26) and clarified that while contemporaneous documentation is vital to resolve factual disputes, Question 5 is not an extra-statutory condition precedent that automatically defeats a claim if written records are incomplete (Joel Theatrical, para 46; Les Abeilles, para 94).
Clevor Technologies Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 166
Synthesized and applied the five Northwest Hydraulic / C.W. Agencies questions (para 11) in evaluating software and technology development claims.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88

Rejected the taxpayer's argument that the "scientific method" criterion was inapplicable because the words "scientific method" do not appear in subsection 248(1), reaffirming Northwest Hydraulic as settled law.

Justice Rennie affirmed the denial of SR&ED credits for a consulting firm's "Project Tracking System" software, holding that: (1) the Northwest Hydraulic test is binding judicial interpretation of s. 248(1) and not ultra vires; (2) the CRA's August 2021 Guidelines are not binding on courts and still mandate experimental rigour under the "How" requirement; and (3) a judge can evaluate vague, non-methodical records without an expert report.

Allowed $343,449 in SR&ED expenditures and $60,963 in ITCs (plus 2014 claims) for a frozen pie manufacturer. Held that overcoming interlocking food formulation constraints (extending shelf life to 21 days without preservatives while reducing salt/fat and maintaining post-freezing crust integrity) involved technological uncertainty; systematically analyzing why failed batches failed met the scientific method; eliminating failed hypotheses achieved advancement; and credible CEO testimony (Mr. Pandya) with existing records satisfied Question 5.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty The King, 2024 TCC 159 (Amended Jan 17, 2025)

Justice Bodie allowed the 2020 SR&ED appeal for Chrisoda (a canned, room-temperature shelf-stable, cold-pressed juice drink where initial test cans exploded). Held that adapting Chiber (a natural mushroom extract from Chinova Bioworks never previously used outside dairy products) to a canned juice beverage went beyond routine engineering, advanced general food science knowledge, and was supported by researcher notes that—even if difficult for an outsider to decipher—enabled the researchers to track hypotheses, tests, and results.

body.text: 8. Administrative Procedures, Filing Deadlines, Audit Reviews, and Penalties
8.1 Prescribed Forms and the Strict 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline

To access SR&ED tax incentives, a claimant must file prescribed forms containing prescribed information with the CRA on or before its SR&ED reporting deadline. Under subsection 37(11) (for the Section 37 deduction pool) and paragraph 127(9)(m) (for the Section 127 ITC) of the ITA, the SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred.

For corporations, because the T2 return filing-due date is 6 months after the end of the taxation year, adding 12 months establishes an absolute statutory reporting deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year (when a tax year ends on the last day of a month, the deadline is the last day of the 18th month following year-end; e.g., a December 31, 2025 year-end has a T2 due date of June 30, 2026, and an SR&ED reporting deadline of June 30, 2027). For self-employed individuals, adding 12 months to the June 15 T1 filing-due date yields a deadline of June 15 of the following year (17.5 months after the December 31 calendar year-end). For trusts, adding 12 months to the 90-day T3 filing-due date yields a deadline of approximately 15 months after the trust's year-end (e.g., March 30 of the second following year for a December 31 year-end).

If Form T661 containing prescribed information is filed after the 18-month reporting deadline, the claim is statute-barred: the expenditures are not recognized as SR&ED expenditures, cannot be added to the Section 37 pool, and earn zero ITCs. There is no statutory mechanism to extend this deadline, nor can taxpayer relief under subsection 220(3.1) revive a late claim. If Form T661 is filed on time within 18 months, but Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) is filed after the 18-month deadline, the allowable expenditures may still be included in the Section 37 deductible pool, but the claimant forfeits all Section 127 ITCs on those expenditures.
8.2 Complete Inventory of Required Federal SR&ED Tax Forms

cells: Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim

Mandatory 10-part prescribed form: Part 1 (General Info); Part 2 (Project Information, including word-limited technical narratives on Line 242 [Uncertainties], Line 244 [Work Performed], and Line 246 [Advancements]; for national security classified projects, Section B of Part 2 is kept on a separate sheet with a notice letter sent to CRA); Part 3 (Section 37 Expenditures & Pool, including irrevocable Proxy/Traditional election on Lines 160/162); Part 4 (Section 127 Qualified Expenditures); Part 5 (Salary Base & 55% PPA on Line 820); Part 6 (Project Costs on Line 750 & SUE Boxes 788–796); Part 7 (Statistics Canada Data); Part 8 (Checklist); Part 9 (Claim Preparer Info); Part 10 (Certification).
Mandatory prescribed schedule/form for claiming Section 127 ITCs, carrybacks, carryforwards, refunds (Part 12 of T2SCH31), and recapture.
Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit
Supplements Schedule T2SCH31 to allocate the $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit among associated CCPCs.
Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length
Supplements Form T661 to allocate unapplied assistance or contract payments between NAL parties under subsection 127(20) (subject to subsection 127(22) validity rules).
Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length
Supplements Form T661 to transfer qualified expenditures from an NAL performer to an NAL payer under subsection 127(13).
Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED
Supplements Form T661 to allocate the 5 × YMPE specified employee wage cap among associated corporations (filed with certified directors' resolutions or sole shareholder confirmation).
Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)
Supplements Form T661 for each third-party payment made to an approved university, college, research institute, or association.

body.text: 8.3 The CRA Review Process, Pre-Claim Approval, and Service Standards

All filed SR&ED claims undergo risk assessment or random sampling by the CRA. As detailed in The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), a claim cannot be withdrawn once it has been selected for review, because Form T661 and its Part 10 certification form an irrevocable part of the income tax return. The CRA's processing service standard is 180 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim for refundable SR&ED claims selected for review (which the CRA aims to meet 90% of the time; non-refundable claims selected for review do not have a fixed service standard). Under the optional Pre-Claim Approval process introduced in Budget 2025 / Bill C-15, businesses can apply before starting SR&ED work to have proposed projects evaluated for technical eligibility. Claims containing pre-claim approved projects that are selected for expenditure-only review are generally processed within 90 calendar days (unless the executed work differed significantly from the pre-approval or was filed alongside non-approved projects, in which case the standard 180-day full review applies).

Reviews are conducted (predominantly via virtual videoconferencing under the National File Assignment System, or on-site on an exceptional basis) in three steps—(1) Start of the Review (initial contact, issue identification, document requests), (2) Review Meeting & Information Requests (interviews with actual R&D performers, inspection of premises, physical samples, scrap, videos, and software commit logs, with 30-day response timelines for additional queries), and (3) End of the Review (issuance of the written Proposal Package and SR&ED Project Eligibility Report)—by two coordinated specialists:

items: Research and Technology Advisor (RTA): Evaluates technical compliance with subsection 248(1), interviews technical staff, inspects facilities and evidence, and prepares the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, reporting to a Research and Technology Manager (RTM).

Financial Reviewer (FR): Examines labour allocations, materials, contracts, overhead, and accounting records in accordance with the Financial Claim Review Manual, reporting to a Financial Review Manager (FRM).

body.text: 8.4 Statutory Penalties: Claim Preparer Penalties and Gross Negligence (Subsection 163(2))

While missing or incomplete claim preparer disclosures in Part 9 of Form T661 do not disallow the SR&ED claim itself (and are not subject to the 18-month reporting deadline), a $1,000 penalty may be assessed for missing, incomplete, or inaccurate Part 9 information, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable.

More severely, under the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), if the CRA proves on a balance of probabilities that a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, made or participated in a false statement or omission on an SR&ED claim—such as claiming projects with clear evidence knowing no SR&ED occurred, fabricating activities that did not take place, or continuing to claim non-qualifying or unsubstantiated amounts after receiving written CRA warnings—a civil penalty applies under subsection 163(2) of the ITA. Taxpayers remain legally responsible for their claims and subject to subsection 163(2) penalties even when prepared by outside consultants. The gross negligence penalty equals the greater of $100 or 50% of the total of:

items: The understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (where overstated pool deductions and overstated ITCs are deemed deducted first, and taxable income is deemed not to be less than zero in a loss year); plus
Under paragraph 163(2)(d), the entire overstated refund of the Refundable ITC claimed, regardless of what caused the overstatement.

body.text: 8.5 Four-Stage Administrative Dispute Resolution and Judicial Appeal Pathway
When a claimant disagrees with proposed audit adjustments, Canadian law and CRA procedure provide a structured four-stage resolution pathway:

items: 30-Day Written Representations to the Proposal Package: Upon receiving the written Proposal Letter, SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, and Summary of Adjustments, the claimant has 30 days from the date of the proposal letter to submit written representations and additional documentary evidence before a final decision is issued.

Working-Level Escalation to the RTM / FRM: Pursuant to Application Policy Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns (AP 2000-02R), if disagreements are not resolved directly with the RTA or FR, the claimant may escalate concerns to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) or Financial Review Manager (FRM).

Administrative Second Review (Administrative Review): If concerns remain unresolved after speaking with the reviewer and their manager, the claimant may request an Administrative Review following receipt of the proposal package. This is not a second technical or financial review by new reviewers; rather, it verifies procedural fairness—confirming whether the review complied with SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures and whether the claimant was accorded due process.

Formal Notice of Objection and Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada: Once the CRA issues a formal Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, a claimant that disagrees with the final decision has the statutory right to file a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, and subsequently to appeal an adverse confirmation to the Tax Court of Canada.
